newsitem.title: RUSSIA: FOCUS - Chubais says Russian 1997 budget unrealistic.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Chubais says Russian 1997 budget unrealistic.

text.p: Russia's reform chief, dismissing the 1997 budget as unrealistic, promised on Thursday to cut spending and raise over $5 billion through state sell-offs and precious metals sales.

Anatoly Chubais, Russian finance minister, told the upper house of parliament that taxes brought in a mere 39 percent of planned income in the first quarter, although higher than expected customs revenues had made up some of the gap.
He said the government needed to cut spending across the board to offset the lower revenue.

"The monstrous budget crisis is at the root of all the troubles and it throws into question whether the state can perform its functions," Chubais said. "It is not possible to finance all scheduled payments under these circumstances."
He added: "We have to recognise that it is not possible to fulfil this budget."

Ministers have long highlighted low tax revenues and huge wage and pension arrears as Russia's most pressing economic problems, and analysts have said the budget, forced through parliament earlier this year, needed to be revised.

The International Monetary Fund has delayed paying several tranches of a $10 billion three-year loan to Russia because it is worried about the revenue shortfall, although visiting IMF Managing Director Michel Camdessus said earlier this month he was ready to recommend Russia's 1998 economic programme.
But a string of government decrees and the creation of an emergency commission to force tax debtors to pay have done little to bring in extra funds.
The new head of the State Tax Service, Alexander Pochinok, promised in an interview on Thursday that he would be tougher than his predecessors.
"In my opinion the State Tax Service has adopted too mild a policy," Pochinok, previously a senior official in the State Duma lower house of parliament, told Commersant Daily newspaper.

"We need to be much tougher... The moment a taxpayer has money and refuses to pay, we need to exact this money in a tough way. The tax service has to be strong enough to obtain what it is entitled to by law."

Under the Russian budget law, the Duma must approve any government decision to sequester spending -- official jargon for cutting spending on all but so-called protected items like health, education and the military.
But the lower house is dominated by communists and nationalists and many deputies have already said planned spending cuts stand little chance of success.
Chubais is due to address the Duma on April 23, telling deputies how the budget was fulfilled in the first quarter and outlining the sequestration plans.
He said on Thursday the government would raise an extra 30 trillion roubles ($5.2 billion) through privatisation and on shares and precious metals markets.

It was not clear exactly how Chubais, who has already targeted higher privatisation revenues this year, expects to raise this money. But sales of gold and diamonds are traditionally a way to bring money to state coffers.
He said the government would finish work on a new tax code on Thursday and the document would be submitted to the Duma.
"We will do everything we can to get it accepted, but we cannot guarantee that it will be passed in time for the 1998 budget to be drawn up on the basis of this code," he said.
Camdessus has said the IMF will not hand over any extra funds until the government approves the tax code, aimed at making Russia's convoluted tax system simpler and more workable.
A senior Russian official, speaking on condition that he was not identified, said the IMF was also seeking clear statements from the government about how it would sequester funds.
"There is some optimism (about IMF payments) because of Camdessus' promises, but it is clear that the budget problem has not got any better," he said.

"The IMF insists that the government adopts a sequestration plan and that the government announces that it has not fulfilled the budget and that the budget is not realistic." ($ = 5749 Russian Roubles)
